claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily governed by Al-driven partial ordering into B2-like clusters.
B2-like ordering lowers the free energy relative to disordered BCC.
Cooling rate controls whether ordered regions form or are kinetically inhibited.
The initial material is single-phase BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 equilibrated above its BCC solvus temperature.
Cooling rate will be varied while microstructural evolution is monitored in real time.
The proposed comparison spans cooling rates of approximately 1, 10, and 100 degrees Celsius per second from about 1200 degrees Celsius to room temperature.
The structural mediator consists of B2-like domains involving Al-Ni and possibly Al-Fe pairing within the BCC matrix.
Slower cooling allows local ordering and promotes B2-domain formation or transformation of the high-temperature BCC phase.
Faster cooling limits nucleation and growth of ordered clusters and traps a metastable disordered BCC structure.
Slow cooling will produce substantial B2 or related ordered domains.
Formation of the ordered domains will generate new diffraction peaks and exothermic calorimetric signals.
Rapid quenching will retain more disordered BCC and suppress significant B2 ordering.
The fast-cooling condition serves as the baseline and is expected to show minimal ordering or transformation.
The proposed mechanism applies near Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 above the BCC solvus and within an Al concentration range sufficient for partial ordering.
Transformation kinetics may change with thermomechanical history or composition.
The ordering temperatures and B2 phase fractions at intermediate and fast cooling rates are not defined and may be sensitive to minor composition and processing variations.
CALPHAD predicts significant B2 precipitation and associated elemental partitioning for the tested alloy and cooling programs.
Failure of slow-cooled samples to exhibit B2 superlattice reflections or exothermic ordering signals despite a thermodynamic prediction of stable ordering would invalidate the hypothesis.
